en: An Exegesis on the *Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra* Composed by Zhixu, the Master from Ancient Wu, known as Ouyi I take refuge in the eternally abiding,
Great Compassionate Honored One, Who dispenses provisional and ultimate teachings like medicine according to the ailment.
I also pay homage to the Master Vasubandhu, the author of the treatise, who provides a detailed explanation in accordance with the capacities of beginners.
It is said: Bodhisattva Vasubandhu established seven aspects to define the dharmas to be practiced, thereby explaining the meaning of this sūtra.
His investigations were precise and his exhortations were earnest; from ten thousand ages henceforth, none has been able to add another word. Behold his words:
"For the sake of those bodhisattvas, so that they may know the path of skillful means; because they know that path, the Buddha-dharma shall endure for a long time;
the faults of both ordinary beings and sages shall be extinguished, and the benefit of self and others shall be accomplished. Alas! Such is the profound purport of this sutra.
The Bodhisattva has indeed exhausted his sincerity. Those of dull faculties in the final age who read this Bodhisattva-śāstra may understand it or not; they may be obscured or enlightened.

Although there are the *Yuan-shi jie-yao* (Essential Points by Master Yuan) and the *Hong-shi bu-zhu* (Supplementary Commentary by Master Hong), these still fail to fully encompass the capacities of all practitioners.
Now, disregarding my own mediocrity and folly, I have ventured to provide another commentary, hoping that even those of the common folk will find it easy to join in the recitation.
It is simply a matter of harmony. △ Now, in order to explain this sūtra, it is divided into two major sections: first, the title; second, the entry into the text.
Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the formal explanation of the title; second, the identification of the translator. This is the first part.

In the title *The Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching Sūtra* (*Fo yijiao jing*), the three characters "Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching" (*fo yijiao*) constitute the specific name (*bieming*), while the single character "Sūtra" (*jing*) constitutes the general name (*tongming*).

Within the specific name, "Buddha" refers to the person who speaks (*nengshuo zhi ren*), and "Bequeathed Teaching" refers to the Dharma that is spoken (*suoshuo zhi fa*). Thus, both the person and the Dharma are indicated, as well as the agent and the object.
This is a simultaneous presentation. "Buddha" is translated as "Awakened. Sentient beings have remained in a dream for long kalpas; the Buddha has severed ignorance, like awakening from a dream.
Having awakened himself, he is further able to awaken others. He awakens to all dharmas without exception, reaching ultimate realization;
therefore, he is named Buddha. Furthermore, the mind within a dream cannot be extinguished; this is called "Original Awakening" (*mūla-awakening*). From the very beginning of the dream...

Upon awakening, one realizes that the dream was fundamentally empty; this is called "initial enlightenment" (*ādi-bodhi*). Once awakened from the dream, there is only the single awakened mind, with no second mind;
this is called "ultimate enlightenment" (*niṣṭhā-bodhi*). This nature of awakening is inherently possessed by all sentient beings, without beginning and without end.
Śākyamuni did nothing more than first attain what we all share equally; therefore, he manifested the attainment of the Buddha-way.
"You are our teacher. Furthermore, because we have long been deluded and lacked awakening, you manifest birth and death within the nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
It is like the lunar orb in the sky: when the water is clear, its reflection appears; when the water is turbid, the reflection vanishes."

Therefore, the Buddha truly abides eternally and has never entered parinirvāṇa; he merely proclaimed his entry into extinction for the sake of those of us who are turbid, evil, and ordinary beings, so as to inspire in us a sense of sorrowful longing.
Furthermore, because his great compassion is inexhaustible and his vast salvation is boundless.

Therefore, although he manifested his passing into extinction, he still left behind his bequeathed teachings (*yijiao*) to guide and lead future generations. "Bequeathed" (*yi*) means to hand down; "teachings" (*jiao*) refers to instructions and admonitions. This is comparable to what is called the *Guming* (Testamentary Charge) in Confucian texts, or what is known in worldly terms as a final will (*yizhu*). To act in accordance with them is to be a true Dharma-heir; to fail to follow these instructions is to be a great rebel and an unfilial son. The "Instructions on the Dharma" and the "Instructions on the Constant" are fully explained as they appear in other extensive commentaries.
It is also titled *The Sutra of Brief Instructions Spoken by the Buddha on the Verge of Parinirvāṇa*.

"Verge" (*chui*) refers to the time when he was about to enter, but had not yet entered [parinirvāṇa]. "Parinirvāṇa" (*niepan*) means being free from faults and severed from non-virtue, neither arising nor ceasing.

This meaning consists of four kinds. First is *svabhāva-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvana of intrinsic purity), which refers to the fact that all phenomena are from the beginning characterized by eternal quiescence;
Buddhas and sentient beings are equal and non-dual, neither increasing nor decreasing. This is not discussed in terms of entering or exiting.

Second is *sopadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder), which means that those of the Three Vehicles have already severed the "bondage of the children" consisting of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
However, the fruits upon which they rely—the bondage of body and mind—still remain. This refers to entering the *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) at the time of realizing the fruit;
that is, the three vehicles extinguish the physical form and dissolve wisdom, returning once more to the fundamental essence that is nameless and substanceless.

Now, this discussion specifically concerns the process of entering [this state]. Fourth is *apratisthita-nirvāṇa* (non-abiding nirvana), which refers to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who possess wisdom.

Therefore, because he does not abide in saṃsāra and possesses great compassion, he does not abide in nirvāṇa. Because he does not abide in saṃsāra, he can manifest extinction where there is no extinction;
because he does not abide in nirvāṇa, he can manifest birth where there is no birth. The Buddha has long since realized this non-abiding nirvāṇa;
now, in order to exhaustively deliver those with whom he has a karmic connection, he manifests entry into nirvāṇa without remainder. In reality, however, it is not so.
It is identical to the single cessation and eternal extinction of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Furthermore, there are three meanings of *nirvāṇa*:

first, *prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity), which is the ontological essence of the *dharmakāya*. This is without emergence and without entry. Second, *pariśuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of perfected purity), which is *prajñā*.

Having reached the ultimate exhaustion of delusions, it is in profound union with the true nature. This is a single entry into eternal entry. Third, *upāya-śuddhi-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of purity through skillful means).
Nirvāṇa is liberation. Through skillful means (*upāya*), it manifests various responsive transformations (*nirmāṇa*). This involves repeatedly emerging and entering [the world].

If one correlates the three meanings with the four aforementioned types: "purity of nature" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) is self-nature pure nirvāṇa (*svabhāva-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*), which is also the essence of non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*);
"perfect purity" (*pariśuddhi*) is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of non-abiding nirvāṇa; and "purity of skillful means" (*upāya-viśuddhi*)...
This is precisely the function of *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*. It consists of two types: that with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and that without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
If these are categorized within the stage of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), they are subsumed under "perfect purity" (*pariśuddhi*), as they represent only a small portion of such perfect purity.

Consequently, they merely reveal the partial truth (*ekadeśasatya*) and do not yet reveal the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) or the middle truth (*madhyamasatya*); they only purify the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the suffering of birth and death (*bhavasaṃkleśa*), but do not purify the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*) or ignorance (*avidyā*).
And as for transformation (*pariṇāma*): if it pertains to the stage of the Tathāgata, it is subsumed under the "purity of skillful means" (*upāya-viśuddhi*).

At the time of his initial attainment of enlightenment, he manifested the state of having a remainder of support (*sopadhiśeṣa*) common to the two vehicles; now, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, he manifests the state of having no remainder of support (*nirupadhiśeṣa*) common to the two vehicles.
Regarding the "brief explanation": this is an essential summary in contrast to the extensive explanations given on ordinary occasions; furthermore, it is intended for those of great capacity.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* seen here is presented in an abbreviated form. △ Second, the identification of the translator:
Translated by Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin dynasty.
The state established by the Yao clan is also called Qin; therefore, it is named Yao Qin. "Tripiṭaka" refers to the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma (Śāstras).
The Sūtras elucidate the one mind; the Vinaya regulates the three karmas; the Śāstras open up wisdom and eloquence.

By means of these Three Studies, one guides oneself and others; such a person is called a Dharma Master. Kumārajīva—here translated as "Child Longevity"—is so named because he possessed the virtues of the elderly even during his childhood.
To translate from Sanskrit into Chinese is termed *yi* (translation). Part Two: Entering [the Text] is further divided into three sections. First, the Introductory Section (*nidāna*).
II. The Main Body; III. The Circulation Section. Now, for the first:
Śākyamuni Buddha first turned the wheel of Dharma and delivered Ājñātakauṇḍinya; finally he preached the Dharma and delivered Subhadra.
Those who were to be delivered have all been delivered. Between the twin śāla trees, he was about to enter [nirvāṇa].
Nirvana. At that time, during the middle watch of the night, when all was tranquil and silent, he briefly expounded the essentials of the Dharma for his disciples.
Śākya is translated here as "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren); it is the clan name (*gotra*) of the Buddha. Muni is translated as "Silent Sage" (Jimo); it is the title (*nāman*) of the Buddha.

In terms of the clan name, there are differences in their formal characteristics; therefore, they are referred to in the treatises as "distinctive characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). In terms of the title, however, all... [text continues]

The principle of the Buddha is identical [to that of the śrāvakas]. Therefore, it is termed the "general characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) in the treatises. Furthermore, the Benevolent One (*Sugata*) possesses great compassion and does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
this characteristic is entirely distinct from that of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). He who is silent and still possesses great wisdom and does not abide in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
this characteristic is roughly the same as that of the two vehicles. One who possesses these two characteristics—the general and the particular—is called a Buddha.
The meaning is as explained previously. The treatise judges this phrase to signify that the Dharma Master has achieved ultimate merit.

After the Buddha attained enlightenment, he preached the Dharma for forty-nine years and delivered immeasurable numbers of people. Now, by citing the beginning and the end, the entire course of his life is encompassed.
At the outset, in the Deer Park, he turned the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths three times; Kauṇḍinya was the very first.
They attained deliverance. This continued until the assembly at the time of the Parinirvāṇa, when Subhadra was the last to attain deliverance. Regarding the term "turning the wheel of Dharma":
the Buddha takes the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths realized within his own mind and causes it to enter the minds of all sentient beings;
this is called "turning. Because this Dharma can crush the three obstacles of sentient beings—afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering—it is so named.
This constitutes the wheel. Because Kaundinya heard this Dharma, he perceived the principle of the Four Truths and crossed over the ocean of birth and death; thus it is called "crossing.
The Sanskrit term *Ajñāta* is translated here as "understanding" (*jie*) and also as "no-knowledge" (*wuzhi*). "Understanding" refers to clearly perceiving the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
"No-knowledge" refers to the realization of the principle of the Truth through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), because therein neither subject nor object exists.
Kauṇḍinya is translated as "Fire-vessel" (Agni-kumbha); it was the clan name of the Venerable One.
Subhadra is translated as "Loving the Wise" or "Virtuous and Wise. He was originally a non-Buddhist who resided in the city of Kuśinagara and was one hundred and twenty years old.
Hearing that the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he went to the Buddha’s presence and heard the Eightfold Noble Path, whereby he attained the first fruit [of the path].
He subsequently left the household life; hearing further the Four Noble Truths, he became an arhat.

Regarding these two points—the initial turning of the wheel of Dharma and the final teaching—the treatise calls them "opening the gateway of the Dharma" and "accomplishing ultimate merit. This refers to the deliverance of Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
The two phrases concerning Kauṇḍinya and the conversion of Subhadra are, in the treatise, termed "the disciple’s accomplishment of ultimate merit.
The fact that all those who were to be saved have already been saved clarifies that the Buddha’s wisdom discerns the capacities [of beings] and is ever without forgetfulness.
The multitude who have attained benefit is beyond calculation; in the treatise, this is termed "the accomplishment of the great universal characteristics."
This concludes the section on merits. *Sāla* translates as "firm" or "solid. Regarding the twin trees: there are two trees in each of the four directions;
each tree has one branch in bloom and one withered. Their upper branches join together and their lower roots are interconnected, symbolizing that the four virtues destroy the eight inversions.

Alternatively, if only a single pair is seen, it symbolizes the destruction of the views of annihilationism and eternalism. This difference arises from the varying capacities of sentient beings, whether great or small.
Therefore, they are merely different perspectives. "Midnight" signifies the Middle Way. In the Mahāyāna, that which is neither flourishing nor withered is the Middle Way;
in the Hīnayāna, that which is free from annihilation and free from permanence is the Middle Way. "Silent stillness" refers to the cessation of the sphere of mental activity.
Regarding "soundless": it is the severance of the path of speech. This tetralemma is designated as the ultimate accomplishment of the self-characteristics of cause and effect.
That is to say: the space between the twin trees is the self-characteristic of the cause; being about to enter *nirvāṇa* is the self-characteristic of the cause together with its fruit;
that it was at midnight is the general self-characteristic; and being tranquil and soundless is the self-characteristic of the fruit.

Furthermore, "the various disciples" refers to the distinctions in rank among the principal members of the retinue. "The essentials of the Dharma" refers to the distinctions in rank between mundane and supramundane dharmas.
This phrase in the treatise is intended to distinguish the accomplishment of ultimate merit through the general characteristics [of these categories].
Now, as he was about to enter nirvana, there would be no further meeting; and since it was already the middle watch of the night, it was the appointed time.
It is not much; therefore, I have taken the essentials and spoken briefly to serve as a final admonition.
Truly, it is no less than a drop of blood for every single character. Can the reader not reflect upon this?

△ Second, the main body of the teaching is divided into two parts. First, the exposition of the essential teachings common to the world; second, the exposition of the essential teachings uncommon to the world.
Within the first part, there are three sections: 1. The essential teaching for counteracting wrong actions; 2. The essential teaching for counteracting and ceasing suffering.

The third section concerns the essential methods for counteracting and extinguishing afflictions; it also consists of four parts. First, the fundamental pure precepts are elucidated. Second, the pure precepts of skillful distancing are elucidated. Third, how the precepts can give rise to all merits is elucidated. Fourth, the benefits of practicing the precepts through exhortation are explained. Now, the first [part]: The fundamental pure precepts are as follows: "If one wishes to attain the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha, one must first uphold the pure precepts. This means that if one desires to attain the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of a Buddha, one must first maintain the pure precepts. Why is this? Because the precepts are the foundation for attaining all virtues. Just as a person who has lost their life cannot enjoy any other pleasures, so too, if one violates the precepts, one cannot attain any of the various virtues. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will not fall into the evil realms; if one violates them, one will surely fall into the evil realms. Moreover, by upholding the precepts, one can eliminate all faults and give rise to all merits. Therefore, one should diligently uphold the precepts. If one upholds the precepts, one will be respected by all sentient beings, just as the moon is honored by all people. If one violates the precepts, one will be despised by all sentient beings, just as a withered tree is shunned by all people. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be protected by the heavenly deities, just as a virtuous official is protected by the king. If one violates the precepts, one will be abandoned by the heavenly deities, just as a wicked official is abandoned by the king. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be welcomed by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, just as a filial son is welcomed by his parents. If one violates the precepts, one will be rejected by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, just as an unfilial son is rejected by his parents. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will attain fearlessness, just as a brave soldier is fearless in battle. If one violates the precepts, one will always be fearful, just as a coward is terrified in battle. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will attain peace and happiness, just as a healthy person is free from illness. If one violates the precepts, one will suffer various miseries, just as a sick person suffers from many pains. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will attain rebirth in heaven, just as a good person attains a high station. If one violates the precepts, one will fall into the hells, just as a wicked person falls into a low station. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will attain liberation, just as a traveler reaches their destination. If one violates the precepts, one will wander in saṃsāra, just as a traveler loses their way. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will attain the Dharma-body, just as gold is refined into its essence. If one violates the precepts, one will remain in the body of afflictions, just as ore remains unrefined. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will attain the Buddha-fruit, just as a seed grows into a great tree. If one violates the precepts, one will never attain Buddhahood, just as a rotten seed cannot sprout. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to benefit others, just as a bright lamp illuminates others. If one violates the precepts, one will be unable to benefit others, just as a dark night cannot illuminate anything. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to transform sentient beings, just as a skilled physician cures illnesses. If one violates the precepts, one will be unable to transform sentient beings, just as an incompetent physician cannot cure illnesses. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to inherit the Buddha's lineage, just as a noble heir inherits the throne. If one violates the precepts, one will sever the Buddha's lineage, just as a commoner cannot inherit the throne. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to repay the Buddha's kindness, just as a loyal subject repays the sovereign. If one violates the precepts, one will fail to repay the Buddha's kindness, just as a traitor fails to serve the sovereign. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to fulfill one's vows, just as a boatman reaches the shore. If one violates the precepts, one will be unable to fulfill one's vows, just as a broken boat cannot reach the shore. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to enter the path of the sages, just as a straight road leads to the capital. If one violates the precepts, one will stray from the path of the sages, just as a crooked path leads nowhere. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to dwell in the realm of the Tathāgata, just as a bird dwells in its own nest. If one violates the precepts, one will dwell in the realm of Māra, just as a bird is trapped in a cage. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to attain the three bodies, just as a precious gem contains all colors. If one violates the precepts, one will be unable to attain the three bodies, just as a common stone lacks luster. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to manifest the ten powers, just as the sun manifests its light. If one violates the precepts, one will be unable to manifest the ten powers, just as the sun is obscured by clouds. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to turn the wheel of the Dharma, just as a great king turns the wheel of authority. If one violates the precepts, one will be unable to turn the wheel of the Dharma, just as a weak king cannot turn the wheel. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to subdue Māra, just as a hero subdues enemies. If one violates the precepts, one will be subdued by Māra, just as a coward is subdued by enemies. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to destroy the army of afflictions, just as a general destroys the enemy host. If one violates the precepts, one will be destroyed by the army of afflictions, just as a defeated general is slain by the enemy. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to attain the ultimate fruit, just as a farmer harvests the grain. If one violates the precepts, one will never attain the ultimate fruit, just as a farmer who neglects the field yields no harvest. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to transcend birth and death, just as a bridge crosses over a river. If one violates the precepts, one will be bound within birth and death, just as a prisoner is confined in a dungeon. Furthermore, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to attain the state of non-retrogression, just as a mountain peak is firm and immovable. If one violates the precepts, one will fall back into the three realms, just as a mountain crumbles and collapses. Moreover, if one upholds the precepts, one will be able to attain the stage of non-arising, just as a diamond is indestructible. If one violates the precepts, one will be subject to arising and ceasing, just as ice melts and flows away. If one violates the precepts, one will remain in the stage of the heterodox, just as a rebel remains outside the court. "You, bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, should revere, treasure, and honor the Prātimokṣa as those who encounter light in darkness or as a poor man who finds a treasure.
You should know that this is your great teacher; there is no difference between this and me remaining in the world."

"Bhikṣu" is translated here as "remover of poverty," which is a designation for a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Furthermore, it contains three meanings: first, "terrorizer of Māra"; second, "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*);

and third, "destroyer of evil. Now, although the Buddha’s bequeathed teachings universally admonish all four assemblies of disciples, the reason why the *sūtras* frequently single out the bhikṣu is also due to three reasons. The first is to demonstrate detachment.
First, because it concerns characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Second, because it demonstrates the path of skillful means (*upāya-mārga*) of the Mahāyāna, which is shared with the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).
Third, because the bhikṣu is the leader of the fourfold assembly; by mentioning their leader, the fourfold assembly is encompassed, as they all likewise practice the conduct of detachment.
Regarding the phrase "after his parinirvāṇa," this indicates the meaning of the bequeathed teaching. *Prātimokṣa* is translated here as "protection" (*bao*).
It is translated as "liberation" (*vimukti*). It is also rendered as "individual liberation" (*prātimokṣa*) or "liberation in every respect.

This is the dharma that is never exhausted or extinguished. Relying upon this *dharmakāya*, one transcends two kinds of obstacles: by attaining transcendence from the obscuration of the darkness of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said, "like encountering light in the dark";
by attaining transcendence from the obscuration of lacking the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), it is said, "like a poor person obtaining treasure. While the Buddha was in the world...

At that time, one takes the Buddha as teacher; after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one takes the precepts as teacher. If one cannot uphold the precepts, then even those in the same hall are separated by ten thousand li.
If one can indeed uphold the precepts, then what difference is there between being a hundred generations apart and being at the same time?

Such are the sincere words from the Golden Mouth. How can one abandon this and seek elsewhere? Next, the expedient means for distancing oneself from [transgressions] to maintain pure precepts is explained.
Those who uphold the pure precepts must not engage in buying and selling or trade. They must not acquire fields or houses, nor keep people as servants, slaves, or livestock.
All forms of planting and all manner of wealth and treasures should be avoided from afar, as if shunning a pit of fire.

They must not cut down grasses or trees, nor dig up the earth or soil. They must not compound medicinal decoctions, practice divination for good or ill fortune, or gaze upward at the stars and constellations.

Astrological calculations of the waxing and waning of the moon, calendrical computations, and mathematical reckonings are all inappropriate for him. He should restrain his body and moderate his food, living in purity and self-sufficiency.

He must not involve himself in worldly affairs or serve as a messenger. He must not practice incantations or seek elixirs of immortality, nor cultivate intimacy with the noble and powerful, nor engage in familiar or disrespectful conduct.
He should instead rectify his own mind and maintain right mindfulness in seeking liberation; he must not conceal any flaws or blemishes.
To manifest eccentricities and delude the masses; regarding the four types of offerings, one should know moderation and contentment, accepting whatever provisions are obtained without hoarding them.
Within this, there are two sections of text: from the beginning up to "digging the earth" is for protecting the precepts so as not to be like ordinary people who increase their transgressions;
from "divining signs" up to "should not hoard" is for protecting the precepts so as not to be like outsiders.
The Path diminishes wisdom. In the beginning, there are generally eleven matters. First, one must not engage in hawking; this is an increase in fault through seeking profit by indirect means.

Second, one must not engage in selling; this is an increase in fault through seeking profit directly before one's eyes. Third, one must not engage in bartering; this is an increase in fault through seeking profit through exchange.
If one follows the prevailing market price without the intention to seek profit, there is no offense. These are the rules for buying and selling.
As explained at length in the Vinaya: (4) One must not acquire fields or houses; this is an increase in faults because such occupations for one’s livelihood lead to the pursuit of excessive security.
(5) One must not maintain a retinue of people; this is an increase in faults regarding kinsmen, as it refers here to external associates rather than those who share the same resolve.
(6) One must not keep slaves or servants; this is an increase in faults because it gives rise to a difficult-to-abandon sense of inferiority.
Because it is easy for such people as these to give rise to pride, (7) one must not keep livestock; this increases faults by seeking profit through raising animals.
(8) One must not engage in any cultivation of plants; this increases faults by increasing busywork. (9) One must not possess various treasures and wealth;
this increases faults by increasing accumulation. (10) One should distance oneself from all of these as one would avoid a pit of fire. This is...
One should not fail to recognize the increase of faults. Eleventh, one must not cut down grass or trees, nor plow the soil or dig the earth;
this is because it is contrary to dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) and causes harm to sentient beings, thereby increasing faults.

Regarding these eleven types of matters that increase faults, a practicing Bodhisattva should swiftly distance himself from them and should not associate with them. However, there may be instances where they are permitted for the sake of the community, as fully explained in the Vinaya.

One must be extremely careful and discerning. In the second section of the text, there are first five matters that are generally prohibited, followed by an explanation of the *Prātimokṣa* regarding three locations.
Regarding the first five matters: (1) one must not compound medicinal decoctions; (2) one must not practice divination for good or bad fortune; (3) one must not gaze upward at the constellations;
(4) one must not calculate the waxing and waning of the moon through astronomical observation; (5) one must not engage in calendrical calculations. All of these...
This is prohibited because those with deviant minds seek profit and fail to comprehend the Dharma of correct causes and conditions.
Next, regarding the body’s abiding in the *prātimokṣa*, there are five points: first, moderation in food, which counteracts the obstacle of others seeking one's own negligence;
second, eating at the proper time, which counteracts the obstacle of insatiability regarding internal sustenance; third, pure livelihood, which counteracts the obstacle of mutual pursuit [of gain].
Seeking obstacles. Fourth, one must not involve oneself in worldly affairs; this is by nature a cessation of excessive activity.
Fifth, one must not act as a messenger; this is by nature a matter of maintaining dignity and not performing menial tasks.
Next, regarding the *prātimokṣa* for the sphere of speech, there are two kinds of wrong speech that should not be committed: first, speech based on false doctrines, namely, sorcery.
Speech that distresses sentient beings; and worldly, improper speech based on false medicines—namely, incantations and elixirs of the immortals.
Second, speech based on false persons: this refers to associating with those of noble lineage and engaging frequently in vulgar and indecent talk.

Furthermore, regarding associating with one's kinsmen, there is much talk of *māna* (conceit). This refers specifically to forming close, intimate, and disrespectful bonds with noble and high-ranking persons.
Next is the *prātimokṣa* concerning the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*), which consists of six points: first, one should rectify one’s own mind;

this serves as an antidote to the obstacle of frequently observing the faults of others, for by not transgressing, one purifies one’s own mind. Second, one should seek liberation through right mindfulness; this serves as an antidote...
1. The obstacle of improper reflection (*mithyā-manasikāra*), because one must be able to transcend the lower stages by oneself.
2. One must not conceal flaws or blemishes; one must not defile the pure precepts, for one does not harbor mental impurities. 3. One must not manifest extraordinary feats to delude the masses;

one must remain far removed from displaying superior practices without cause, lest it lead others to incorrect understanding. 4. Regarding the four types of offerings, one must know moderation and be content.

It serves as the antidote to the obstacle of being limitless and insatiable in the enjoyment of requisites: for if one enters the factors of meditative concentration (*samādhi-aṅga*), one knows moderation;
and if one enters the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), one is content. The four types of offerings consist of food and drink, and clothing.

Requisites such as bedding and medicine—these six types of offerings should not be accumulated. This is because one must remain far removed from the mind of covetousness that hoards various possessions.

By means of these skillful methods, one distances oneself from the faults of ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists, thereby purifying the aggregate of precepts (*śīlaskandha*) and becoming capable of succeeding to the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body. △ Third, it clarifies how the precepts can give rise to all [virtues].
This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of upholding the precepts. The precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly conforming to liberation; therefore, they are called *pratimokṣa*.
By relying upon these precepts, one attains various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
The essence of the precepts is one alone, namely, non-action (*avijñapti*). The manifestations of the precepts are exceedingly numerous, namely, the five categories and seven groups.
Now, speaking of those most easily transgressed by common sentiment, this is called a "concise exposition.

Because of these precepts, one is able to cross to the other shore from the evils of body, speech, and mind, thereby accomplishing liberation through the three karmas. Therefore, if a practitioner desires to correctly...
For those who follow liberation, this precept must necessarily be taken as the foundation. From the precepts arises concentration; from concentration arises wisdom.
There is no concentration or wisdom that does not arise from the precepts. △ Fourth, the explanation of the benefits of practicing the precepts.
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should maintain pure precepts and not allow them to be broken or deficient. If a person can maintain pure precepts, they will be able to possess wholesome dharmas;
if there are no pure precepts, none of the various wholesome merits can arise. For this reason, you should know.
Precepts are the foremost dwelling place for the merit of peace and security.
Within this, there are five exhortations: first, one should maintain pure precepts; this exhorts one not to lose one's own essence.
Second, do not allow them to be broken or deficient; this exhorts one not to abandon skillful means. Third, being able to possess wholesome dharmas; this exhorts one to constantly accumulate merit.
Virtue. Fourth, if one lacks pure precepts and so forth, this is an exhortation to recognize the many faults and evils [of such a state].
Fifth, it is the dwelling place of the merit of peace and security; this is an exhortation to dwell in a state of peace and security, and not to dwell in a state of insecurity.

The first section on the essential method for counteracting wrong actions is complete. △ Second, the three essential methods for counteracting and ceasing suffering. First, the suffering of the senses, desires, and negligence.

The remedies: (1) the remedy for the suffering of overeating; (2) the remedy for the suffering of sloth and sleep; and (3) [the remedy for] the initial two. Regarding the first of these, there are two:
(a) the remedy for the suffering of sensory indulgence, and (b) the remedy for the suffering of desire-driven indulgence. Now, the first [of these].
"O bhikṣus, since you have already been able to abide in the precepts, you must now restrain the five faculties so that they do not become heedless and enter into the five desires.
It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over his cattle, not allowing them to run wild and trespass upon the crops.
If you let the five faculties run loose, it will not be merely the five desires; they will become boundless and impossible to restrain. It would be like a vicious horse that is not [restrained]..."
The bit and reins are intended to restrain a person from falling into a pit or ditch; such suffering caused by bandits lasts but a single lifetime.
However, the calamity of the thieves that are the five sense faculties brings disaster upon successive generations; their harm is exceedingly grave, and one must not fail to be cautious.

Therefore, the wise restrain them and do not follow after them, holding them as they would a thief, not allowing them to run wild. Even if one were to let them loose, they will all soon reveal their [true nature].
"Exhausted. This refers to having already been able to abide in the precepts, speaking of the two types previously mentioned: the fundamental [precepts] and the preparatory means.

Below, the essential method for guarding the sense faculties is correctly explained through three metaphors. First, the section beginning with "One should restrain the five sense faculties" is the metaphor of the cowherd. First, the application of the Dharma (the analogy).
The subsequent analogy concerns the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), namely: eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; and the five objects of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*), namely:
form, sound, odor, taste, and touch. The ox represents the five sense faculties; the herdsman represents the bhikṣu; the held staff represents the mindfulness of ethical discipline (*śīla-smṛti*);

and the crops represent all virtuous qualities, namely the dharmas such as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Next, the passage beginning with "If one indulges the five sense faculties" and so forth is the analogy of the evil horse. This also first...

The Dharma. The subsequent analogy: the "evil horse" also represents the five sense-faculties (*pañcendriya*); the "reins that restrain" also represent ethical discipline (*śīla*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*).
The "pitfall" represents the three evil realms (*trividha-durgati*). If one lets loose the five sense-faculties, it not only obstructs the wholesome, but inevitably leads to falling into evil.

Therefore, it is said: "not only do the five desires have no limit. Regarding the passage "like being robbed by bandits" and so forth, this is the analogy of the bandits; first the analogy, then [the application].

The Dharma: its calamities extend through successive generations; its misfortune is more severe than that of a bandit. If one does not restrain oneself and instead follows [the senses], how can one be called wise?

Furthermore, even if one were to indulge them, they will soon perish, like honey on the edge of a blade—insufficient for even a single meal, yet if a child licks it, he suffers only the calamity of having his tongue cut. △ Second, the desire for indulgence and negligence.
As for the antidote to suffering, these five faculties have the mind as their master. Therefore, you all should properly restrain the mind.

The mind is more fearsome than a venomous snake, a wild beast, or a hostile thief; even a great conflagration spreading out of control is insufficient to serve as a metaphor for it. It is, for example, like a person...
Holding a vessel of honey, he moves about with restless haste; he gazes only at the honey and does not see the deep pit.
Like a mad elephant without a hook, or a monkey that has found a tree—leaping, bounding, and scrambling about, difficult to restrain—one must swiftly subdue it so that it does not become dissolute.
To let this mind run wild destroys a person’s wholesome deeds; to control it in a single place, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished. Therefore:
"O bhikṣu, you should exert yourself with diligence and subdue your own mind.
The five sense-faculties are material phenomena; they are dull and devoid of consciousness, functioning only in dependence upon the mind. Therefore, the mind is their master."
Therefore, if one wishes to restrain the five sense faculties, nothing is equal to restraining the mind.
Regarding what is called "skillfully restraining the mind," one should know that this mind possesses three kinds of characteristics of samādhi and three kinds of obstructing factors.

First is the obstruction of the differentiation of the mind's nature, which can obstruct the samādhi of non-dual mindfulness. Second is the obstruction of lightness, agitation, and lack of discipline, which can obstruct pliancy and immovability.
Samādhi. Third is the obstacle of losing all meritorious qualities (*guṇa*). This can obstruct the arising of samādhis that produce manifold merits.

In the text, the passage beginning with "the mind's dreadfulness" first clarifies the obstacles regarding the differentiation of the nature of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*). The afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to the category of greed (*rāga*) suck up and consume the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), being more dangerous than venomous snakes.
The afflictions belonging to the category of hatred (*dveṣa*) swallow and destroy the roots of goodness, being more ferocious than predatory beasts. The category of delusion (*moha*)...

The afflictions (*kleśa*) damage and destroy the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) more than an enemy or thief; the "equal-part" afflictions (*samabhāga-kleśa*) incinerate the roots of goodness more than a runaway great fire.
Therefore, it is said that no analogy is sufficient. Next, the passage beginning with "Suppose there were a person... clarifies the obstacle of being restless and undisciplined.

The vessel of honey is a metaphor for the five faculties (*indriya*) experiencing the pleasures of the five sense objects (*viṣaya*); their shifting and light fickleness is a metaphor for [the mind] turning [toward distraction].

Consciousness follows the various sense faculties, being unstable from moment to moment; it perceives only the honey, which is a metaphor for the six consciousnesses that take only the present six objects as their conditions and do not see the deep pit, which is a metaphor for not knowing future obstacles. There are two kinds of obstacles.

First, there is the obstacle of wasting one's entire life in vain. Second, there is the obstacle of being unable to achieve accomplishment due to the suffering and hardship encountered when practicing all the various deeds.
A mad elephant without a hook is a metaphor for the mind that is not restrained by the dharma of samādhi.

A monkey that has found a tree is a metaphor for the mind that gives rise to defilement by taking the six sense-objects as its conditions; therefore, one must urgently subdue it and cause it to enter the unshakable samādhi of pliancy. Next...
"To let this mind run wild causes one to lose all that is wholesome; it clearly obstructs the attainment of all merits.

This is the phrase "restraining it in a single place," which demonstrates the mark of samādhi free from dualistic thought. "There is no task that cannot be accomplished" demonstrates the mark of samādhi that gives rise to manifold merits.
"With diligence, subdue your own mind" demonstrates the mark of samādhi that is pliant, compliant, and immovable. △ Two.
"Eating much is an obstacle to be countered.
You bhikṣus, when receiving various foods and drinks, should regard them as taking medicine; whether they are good or bad, do not give rise to feelings of attachment or aversion."

One should obtain what is necessary merely to sustain the body and eliminate hunger and thirst. Just as a bee gathers from a flower only its nectar without damaging its color or fragrance, so too should a bhikṣu accept the offerings of others only to remove his own afflictions; he must not seek much, lest it destroy his virtuous mind.
For example, it is like a wise person who calculates the extent of an ox’s strength and does not overtax it so as to exhaust its power.

Excessive eating can obstruct *samādhi*; therefore, one should remedy this with the five reflections. First, one should regard food as taking medicine; this is the reflection on the remedy for attachment to enjoyment.
Second, do not give rise to thoughts of increase or decrease; this is the reflection on the equality of the good and the bad. Third, [one should reflect on] the maintenance of the physical body.

Hunger and thirst: this is the contemplation of ultimate remedies. Fourth, the four [contemplations] such as the bee gathering nectar from flowers; first the simile, then the teaching—this is the contemplation of not harming oneself or others.
Fifth, for example, like a wise person weighing the strength of an ox and so forth—this is the contemplation of knowing measure and knowing the proper time.
Medicine is used to treat illness, and food is used to treat hunger; if it can simply treat the hunger, that is sufficient. Why then [is there more]?
When encountering what is pleasant, the mind of craving increases and devours it; when encountering what is unpleasant, the mind of aversion diminishes and consumes it.

"Approaching" (*āya*) means taking up; "supporting" (*apāya*) means sustaining. The bee is a metaphor for the bhikṣu; the flower is a metaphor for offerings; the nectar is a metaphor for utilizing these to cultivate the Path and eliminate afflictions;
the color and fragrance are metaphors for one's own and others' wholesome minds. To greedily consume and seek much [of the nectar] not only damages one’s own samādhi and virtue, but also...
This damages the donor’s wholesome mind. A cow is able to carry heavy loads; however, if the burden exceeds its capacity, its strength will be exhausted.
This is a metaphor for a bhikṣu who, though he serves as a field of merit for the world, will find his path naturally ruined if he greedily accepts excessive offerings.
△ Third, the remedy for the suffering of indolence and sleep.
"O you bhikṣus, during the day you should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas so as not to let the time pass in vain.
During the first watch and the last watch of the night, do not neglect your practice either. In the middle watch, recite the sūtras to rest your body and mind.
Do not, on account of sleep, allow this one life to pass empty-handed without attainment. You should reflect that the fire of impermanence burns all worlds; seek liberation for yourselves early."
"Cross over! Do not succumb to sleep. The thieves of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) constantly lie in wait to kill you;

they are more dangerous than an enemy. How can you sleep so soundly without awakening yourself? The venomous snake of affliction sleeps within your heart. It is like a black viper sleeping in your room;
you must use the hook of moral discipline (*śīla*) to expel it as soon as possible. Only when the sleeping snake has been driven out may you sleep in peace."
To go out and sleep is the mark of a person devoid of shame (*ahrīka*). The garment of shame is the foremost among all forms of adornment.
Shame is like an iron hook, capable of restraining a person from what is unrighteous. Therefore, one should always maintain a sense of shame and never allow it to lapse for even a moment.

If one is separated from shame, then all virtuous qualities are lost. One who possesses a sense of moral dread (*ottappa*) possesses wholesome states; if one lacks moral dread, they are [no different from]...
There is no difference between these various birds and beasts.
Because the mind is indolent, there is sloth; because the body is weary and heavy, there is drowsiness.

These two characteristics accord with one another, together forming a single affliction that obstructs concentration and wisdom, preventing them from arising. Furthermore, this drowsiness arises from three factors. First, from...

Sleep arises from three causes: first, from food; second, from the time of day; and third, from the mind. In the Sūtra, it says, "Diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas so as not to let the proper time pass," which is the remedy for sleep arising from food.
The passage beginning with "In the first watch and the last watch of the night, do not allow for negligence" and so forth, is the remedy for sleep arising from the time of day.
From "One should contemplate the fire of impermanence" onwards, all [is the remedy for sleep arising from the mind].

There are two further intentions regarding the counteracting of sleep that arises from the mind. First, from "one should contemplate impermanence" up to "not awakening through self-alertness," this is the counteractive of analytical observation (*vipaśyanā-pratipakṣa*).
Second, from "the poisonous snake of afflictions" up to "there is no difference from the signless (*animitta*)," this is the counteractive of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-pratipakṣa*).
Within the first, the counteractive of analytical observation, there are two types of impermanence. The first is...
Arising and ceasing over a period of time is coarse; arising and ceasing in every moment is subtle. The mundane world is also twofold:

first, the dependent retribution of the three realms, which is the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*); second, the primary retribution of the six destinies, which is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*).
Both the primary and secondary worlds are subject to total extinction; nothing can remain. Thus, they are like a conflagration.

Furthermore, regarding the two types of afflictions—craving and views—within the three realms and nine stages, there are eighty-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of views and eighty-one grades of craving.
There is nothing among these that cannot wound the *dharmakāya* and destroy the life-force of wisdom; therefore, they are even more grievous than an enemy. It is thus.
"Observation and awakening" is termed the "observation as an antidote. Next, regarding the antidote of pure morality:
although afflictions do not manifest at present, they have never failed to lie dormant and slumbering within your storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
These afflictions are poisonous and terrifying, like black vipers; if they do not arise, that is one thing, but once they arise, they will inevitably kill you according to their nature.

The body is the vessel for the life of wisdom; were it not for the hook of ethical discipline (*śīla*), how could one eliminate both [the body and its afflictions] together? As for the "hook of discipline," the *prātimokṣa* precepts can guard the body and speech;
the discipline concomitant with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*) can subdue mental delusions; and the discipline concomitant with the Path (*mārga-samvara*) can sever mental delusions.
Possessing these three precepts, one eternally extinguishes the seeds of affliction within the field of the eight consciousnesses; this is called "the sleeping snake having finally emerged.
From this point on, what remains to be done is accomplished, and one no longer undergoes future existence; this is called "being able to sleep in peace.

Therefore, although an Arhat has severed the sleep of the mind, they do not sever the sleep that arises from eating or the sleep that arises according to the seasons, for those forms of sleep do not [constitute the afflictions].
Because they act as hindrances: if one now falls asleep while the seeds of affliction have not yet been severed, one fails to respect one's own spiritual nature;
this is called *āhrīkya* (lack of shame). Not feeling ashamed of one’s own faults and evils is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of remorse).

Furthermore, not aspiring toward the sages and worthies is called *āhrīkya*; not being ashamed of base and low conduct is called *anapatrāpya*. These two virtues, *hrī* and *apatrāpya*, [are essential].
The mental factors (caitta) necessarily arise simultaneously [with the mind]. That which distinguishes humans from birds and beasts lies precisely herein; should one not strive in this? Section Two:
The Essentials of the Method for Stopping Suffering through Antidotes is concluded. △ Section Three: The Essentials of the Method for Extinguishing Afflictions through Antidotes has three parts:
First, the antidote for the afflictive hindrance of anger; Second, the antidote for the afflictive hindrance of arrogance; Third...
First, regarding the antidote for the afflictive hindrance of flattery and crookedness:
"O bhikṣus, if someone were to come and sever your body limb by limb, you should restrain your own minds and not allow anger or resentment to arise."
You must also guard your speech and refrain from uttering evil words. If you give rein to a heart of anger, you will obstruct your own path and lose the benefits of merit.
The virtue of patience is such that it cannot be equaled by the observance of precepts or ascetic practices. One who is able to practice patience may be called a powerful great being.
If one cannot joyfully endure the poison of foul abuse as if drinking ambrosia, [one is not yet a true practitioner].
Such a person is not called one who has entered the Way or a person of wisdom. Why is this? The harm of anger destroys all wholesome dharmas and ruins a good reputation;
in both this life and future lives, people take no pleasure in seeing such a person. You should know that the angry mind is more fierce than a raging fire;

you must always guard against it so that it does not gain entry. No thief of merit surpasses anger. (For laypeople) *Note: The phrase "白衣" (*bāiyī*) at the end indicates that this passage concludes a section addressed to lay practitioners.*
Those who indulge in sensual desires and are not practitioners of the Way, lacking self-restraint, may have their anger somewhat excused.

However, for those who have left the household life to practice the Way and are free from desire, to harbor anger is utterly improper; it is like lightning striking and fire erupting from within clear, cool clouds.
This is not what is appropriate.
The text consists of six sections. The first, "If someone were to come and sever one's limbs joint by joint," sets forth the objects of endurance;
it uses the heavy to illustrate the light, showing that if even limb-severing is to be endured, how much less should other adverse conditions cause one concern? Next...
"Should restrain one's own mind," and so forth, correctly demonstrates the characteristics of forbearance. By not allowing anger or resentment to arise, one’s body and mind become pure;
by refraining from uttering evil words, one’s verbal karma becomes pure. Third, "if one indulges the heart of wrath," and so forth, clarifies the faults of non-forbearance.
That which "hinders one’s own path" means one cannot achieve self-benefit; that which "loses the benefit of merit" means one cannot benefit others.
When anger arises, both self-interest and the welfare of others are lost; this clearly demonstrates that it must not be indulged.
Regarding the virtue of the four types of patience (*kṣānti*), he deeply extols its supreme power to encourage practice.

Indeed, one who observes the precepts (*śīla*) is not necessarily able to practice patience, but one who practices patience will certainly never fail to observe the precepts. This is why, among the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), ethical discipline occupies the second position.
Patience (*kṣānti*) occupies the third stage. This is because the preceding stages do not encompass the subsequent ones, whereas the subsequent stages necessarily include the preceding ones.

If one observes the precepts with a sense of self, the retribution will be limited to the realms of humans and devas; yet, if one practices patience without a sense of self, it becomes the Great Path that transcends the world.
To suffer offense without seeking retribution is like the vastness of the ocean and the open sky, where one allows the hawk to soar and the fish to leap as they please; therefore, it is so named.
A person of great power. Fifth, if one is unable to [practice equanimity], it serves to further clarify the fault of failing to practice patience (*kṣānti*) as a warning to practitioners.
Ambrosia (*amṛta*) is the medicine of immortality; through the malicious abuse of others, my power of patience is perfected.
It is like a pig rubbing against a mountain of gold—the gold becomes all the more radiant—or a stone grinding a fine sword—the sword becomes all the more sharp. Thus, King Kali...

All of them are true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) of Śākyamuni. If one does not regard harsh abuse as nectar (amṛta), and cannot joyfully endure it, this is indeed folly, for one has not yet heard the Way.

How much more so when a single thought of anger arises and a million gates of obstruction open, destroying all wholesome dharmas—how could one then benefit oneself? It ruins one’s good reputation; how could one... [then benefit others]?
Benefiting others. In this life there is no cause for the two benefits; in future lives there will be no fruit of the two benefits. Who would take pleasure in seeing such a thing?

Therefore, wishing to protect the wholesome dharmas of self-benefit, one should guard against the fire of anger; wishing to protect the merit of benefiting others, one should guard against the thief of anger.
Regarding the six laypeople who indulge in desires and so forth, the conclusion is that they are inappropriate; this follows from the person.
Those among the inhabitants of the six heavens of the desire realm who have not yet entered the Path are all called "white-robed. They possess two faults:

first, they indulge in sensual desires; since desire and hatred are mutually reinforcing, [the former leads to the latter]. Second, they do not practice the Path and lack wholesome dharmas to restrain the mind.
Therefore, while hatred may still be somewhat excusable—it being said that for laypeople to commit offenses is within their natural lot—it is not something to be deeply censured.

One who has left the household life to practice the Way should be free from desire, like a clear and cool cloud; how could they harbor a mind of anger and resentment, as if igniting the fire of a thunderclap?
△ Second, the antidote for the afflictive hindrance of arrogance.
"O bhikṣus, you should rub your own heads; for you have already abandoned ornaments and fine clothing, donned dyed robes, and taken up alms-bowls to sustain yourselves by begging.
Seeing yourselves in this way, if arrogance should arise, you must quickly extinguish it. Do not allow arrogance to increase."
This is not even appropriate for worldly laypeople, let alone for those who have left the household life to enter the Path.
For the sake of liberation, why would they humble themselves to go begging?
The text consists of two sections. The first, beginning with "You, bhikṣus," correctly establishes the remedy. The second, beginning with "Increasing arrogance," compares what is inappropriate.
Within the first section, there are five phrases of remedy: 1) One should rub one's own head, as there is no crown or tiara to adorn it;
2) Having already discarded ornaments, there are no swords or pendants to decorate the body; 3) Wearing...
As for wearing robes of dyed color, one does not have the five colors to brighten one's attire.
As for holding the alms-bowl, one has no servants to perform services. As for sustaining oneself by begging, one has no treasury to accumulate wealth.
Therefore, one should constantly observe with wisdom; should pride arise, one must immediately and swiftly eliminate it. [Wearing] dyed color...

Regarding robes: these consist of the three types of *kāṣāya* as well as all items such as lower garments and sitting mats, all of which must be dyed with one of the three "defiled" colors—blue, black, or madder.
Regarding the vessel: this refers to the *pātra*; its material, color, and dimensions must all accord with the Dharma.
Its substance consists solely of two things: clay and iron; its color is stained like that of a pigeon; and its size corresponds to the capacity of the stomach.
Next, the text cites the example of a layperson (śrāvaka) for comparison: if even a layperson should not harbor arrogance, how much more so one who seeks liberation?
△ Third, the antidote to the afflictive hindrance of flattery and crookedness.
"O bhikṣus, a mind of flattery and crookedness is contrary to the Way. Therefore, you should make your minds upright and sincere.
You should know that flattery and crookedness serve only for deception; for one who has entered the Way, such things have no place.
For this reason, you should straighten your hearts and take up sincerity as your foundation."
Words that seek to flatter and accommodate others are called *ch'an* (flattery). Thoughts that waver and twist according to circumstances are called *ch'ü* (crookedness).

Flattery implies a lack of sincerity; crookedness implies a lack of integrity. These lead only to self-deception and the deception of others; they are certainly not the attributes of one who enters the Path.
A straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); because the mind and its words are straightforward, there will forever be no trace of deviousness.

If one does not maintain right mindfulness of *tathatā* (suchness), how can one be said to have a rectified mind? The first section, clarifying the essential dharmas shared with the world, is concluded.
△ Second, clarifying the essential dharmas not shared with the world. This refers to the accomplishment of the supramundane merits of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).
The text is divided into eight parts: first, the merit of having no seeking; second, the merit of contentment; third, detachment...
The merit of virtue; fourth, the merit of tirelessness; fifth, the merit of non-forgetfulness; sixth, the merit of meditative concentration;
seventh, the merit of wisdom; eighth, the merit of ultimate perfection. Now, the first:
"O bhikṣus, you should know that for those who have many desires, because they seek many gains, their suffering and affliction are also many.
For those with few desires, being without seeking and without desire, these afflictions do not exist. One should cultivate even this state of having few desires;
how much more so since having few desires can give rise to all manner of meritorious qualities. A person with few desires has no flattery or crookedness in order to seek the favor of others."
Furthermore, one who is not led astray by the sense faculties and practices few desires will have a mind that is serene, free from anxiety and fear.
In all matters, they will find abundance and never feel lacking. Where there is fewness of desire, there is *nirvāṇa*; this is called "fewness of desire."
The text contains five kinds of characteristics for knowing and awakening. First is the characteristic of knowing and awakening to obstacles:

that is, excessive desire is the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); excessive seeking is the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*); and excessive suffering and distress are also largely the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). Second is the characteristic of knowing and awakening to remedies.
This means that if one is without seeking and without desire, then these afflictions do not exist. Third, knowing the characteristic of the arising of causes and conditions through perception:

this means that having few desires is free from affliction; since this should already be cultivated, how much more so when it can give rise to all merits and accomplish immeasurable noble and wholesome dharmas?
Fourth, knowing the characteristic of ultimate freedom from all obstacles through perception: this means being without flattery or crookedness, which is the absence of delusion.
There is no obstruction of karma, for there is no intention to seek [rebirth]. There is no obstruction of suffering, for one is not led astray by the sense faculties.
This is because the eye faculty leads a person to experience forms, and so on until the body faculty leads a person to experience tangibles;

these cause one to lose self-mastery and constitute great suffering. This is the mark of the accomplishment of the fruit of the five types of clear comprehension (*pañca-abhijñā-phala*): namely, that the mind is then serene and composed.
The accomplishment of the Dharma-body is such that there is no anxiety or fear; this is the accomplishment of Prajñā.
To encounter all matters with abundance and always lack nothing is the accomplishment of Vimukti. The full possession of these three virtues is called Mahāparinirvāṇa.
Thus, it is known that having few desires is the cause and Nirvāṇa is the fruit. △ Second, the merit of contentment.
"O bhikṣus, if you wish to be liberated from all suffering and affliction, you should contemplate contentment.
The dharma of contentment is itself the place of wealth, joy, peace, and security. For one who is content, even though they lie upon the bare ground, they are still at ease and happy.
For one who lacks contentment, even though they dwell in heaven, it is not to their satisfaction. One who lacks contentment is poor despite being wealthy; one who is content is rich."
Such a person, though poor, is rich; whereas one who does not know contentment is constantly led astray by the five desires and is pitied by those who do know contentment. This is called contentment.

The former, "merit through seeking nothing," refers to distancing oneself from the sphere of others' affairs. The present, "merit through contentment," refers to distancing oneself from one's own affairs.
Within the text, "desiring to escape suffering and affliction" serves as the remedy for the causes and effects of suffering;
"wealth, joy, and tranquility" further explains the causes and effects of purity. Next, the stages of the earth (*bhūmi*) are contrasted with the heavenly realms. This is...
The distinctions are demonstrated by way of two points. Furthermore, the contrast between the wealthy and the poor demonstrates the distinction by way of these two matters.
Moreover, the contrast between being dragged away by desire and having compassion demonstrates the distinction by way of two dharmas:
one has no self-benefit, while the other possesses both self-benefit and benefit for others. One is constantly dragged away by the five desires; this is the absence of self-benefit. One...
Thus, one is not led astray by the five desires; this is self-benefit. Furthermore, being able to have compassion for those who lack contentment is benefit for others.
△ Third, the merit of distancing oneself [from faults].
"O bhikṣus, those of you who seek tranquility, the unconditioned, and peace and happiness, should distance yourselves from clamor and dwell alone in seclusion.
One who dwells in such stillness is revered by Śakra and all the devas; therefore, you should abandon both your own group and other groups."
Dwelling alone in seclusion, one contemplates the eradication of the root of suffering. If one delights in the company of others, one will undergo manifold afflictions.
It is like a great tree: when flocks of birds gather upon it, there is the peril of withering and breaking.
Those bound and attached to the world are submerged in manifold sufferings, just as an old elephant mired in mud cannot extricate itself. This is called "separation."

The text comprises three gates that encompass its meaning. First is the gate of the essential nature of detachment. Because its substance is transcendent, it manifests four kinds of antidotes: namely, tranquility, the unconditioned, and bliss.
These serve as antidotes to the obstacle of attachment to the mark of a self (*ātman*). "Tranquility" refers to the emptiness of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*);
"the unconditioned" refers to the emptiness of signlessness (*animitta-śūnyatā*); and "bliss" refers to the emptiness of the vow of neither grasping nor rejecting (*apranihita-śūnyatā*).

One should distance oneself from clamor and bustle to counteract the obstacle of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*). When the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arise in disorder without sequence, this is termed "clamor.
Dwelling alone in seclusion counteracts those two obstacles of signlessness (*animitta*), namely "I" and "mine," which are fundamentally signless by nature.
By now practicing the three samādhis, one manifests the principle of signlessness, and those obstacles are accordingly extinguished. Śakra.
It is revered by all the devas. It is the foremost merit that counteracts the obstacles to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
A secluded place is a dharma worthy of honor, for it is the most preeminent among all wholesome dharmas. Second is the gate of cultivating seclusion (*viveka*), because it is the means for emergence.

One’s own group refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*). Another’s group refers to teachers, disciples, and fellow students. A quiet and empty place...

Dwelling alone and abiding in accordance with the Dharma is the accomplishment of skillful wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*). Contemplating the cessation of the root of suffering and distancing oneself from its causes is the accomplishment of discerning wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyāna-jñāna*).
Third, regarding the gateway of experiencing various views: because one is constantly bound by them, those who delight in crowds experience manifold afflictions.
The great tree is a metaphor for the sixth consciousness; the flock of birds is a metaphor for the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
This is spoken with reference to one's own assembly: the great tree represents the bhikṣu, and the flock of crows represents his fellow students and disciples.
This is spoken with reference to others' assemblies: from these various views, they arise and gather, which is likened to the calamity of being withered and broken.
Furthermore, because karma is formed on account of views, and suffering is brought forth by karma, it is likened to an old elephant sinking in the mud, unable to extricate itself.
Old age is like the decline of contemplative wisdom; this is the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). The elephant’s massive body is like the thickness of clinging attachment;

this is the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). Sinking into the mud is like being submerged in manifold sufferings; this is the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*). To not distance oneself from these even once [is the nature of the obstacle].
Bound eternally by the three obstacles, how can you not contemplate deeply the essential means of deliverance? △ Fourth, the merit of tirelessness:
"O bhikṣus, if you exert yourselves with diligent vigor, then no task will be difficult. Therefore, you should all be diligent and vigorous.
For example, even a small amount of water, if it flows continuously, can pierce through stone. If the mind of a practitioner repeatedly succumbs to indolence and desists..."
It is like drilling for fire: if one stops before it has grown hot, although one wishes to obtain fire, the fire will be difficult to find.
This is called diligence (*vīrya*): to be diligent is to be free from indolence; to be refined is to be free from distraction; to advance is to be free from regression.

Therefore, the noble fruits of the Three Vehicles are attained without difficulty, unlike the fruitless ascetic practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Next, there is the analogy of a small stream piercing through stone.

The merit of constant, uninterrupted effort is illustrated by the analogy of drilling wood for fire while counting one's breaths; this serves as a metaphor for the faults of indolence and loss of mindfulness, as can be understood from the text.
△ Fifth, the merit of non-forgetfulness of mindfulness.
"O bhikṣus, in seeking a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and seeking wholesome protection and assistance, there is none like non-forgetfulness of mindfulness (asmṛti).
If one possesses non-forgetfulness of mindfulness, the thieves of the various afflictions (kleśa) cannot enter. Therefore, you should always collect and hold mindfulness within the mind.
If one loses mindfulness, one loses all meritorious qualities (guṇa). If the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, even if one enters among the thieves of the five desires (pañcakāmaguṇa)..."
In the midst [of these], one is not harmed. It is like entering a battle array wearing armor; then there is nothing to fear. This is called "unfailing mindfulness" (*asmṛti*).
This unfailing mindfulness is the foremost of all practices. Regarding "all practices," they are briefly explained as being of three kinds.
First, the practice of hearing the Dharma, which is to seek a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). Second, the practice of internal reflection, which is to seek proper protection.
Third, the practice of practicing according to the Dharma, which is to seek virtuous assistance. These three practices are also called the "three wisdoms.

Wisdom has the meaning of illuminating and understanding; practice has the meaning of advancing and progressing. Both illumination and understanding, as well as advancement and progress, all depend upon non-forgetfulness of mindfulness (*asmṛti*).
There is no practice of hearing; like an overturned vessel, it cannot receive water. There is no practice of reflection; like a leaking vessel, though it receives, it loses it.

There is no practice of cultivation; like a defiled vessel, though it does not leak or lose, its filth renders it unusable. Now, if there is mindfulness that does not forget, then these three practices are present.
One who possesses these three practices is able to destroy the enemy of afflictions, which has existed since beginningless time. Therefore:
One should always maintain mindfulness within the heart. Thus donning firm armor and entering the fray, one will not be harmed by the marauders and will be able to slay them.
△ Sixth, the merit of meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi).

"O bhikṣus, if you restrain the mind, the mind will abide in concentration. Because the mind abides in concentration, one is able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of phenomena in the world.
Therefore, you should always diligently practice various forms of concentration. If you attain concentration,"

The mind then does not scatter. Just as a household that cherishes water skillfully maintains its dikes and ponds, so too the practitioner, for the sake of the water of wisdom, skillfully cultivates meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) so that it does not leak away; this is called concentration (*samādhi*).

"Collecting the mind" means that through skillful means, one rebukes and abandons the mental activities of the lower stages, thereby being able to successively realize and enter the various dhyānas, even giving rise to diverse samādhis.
Once the mind is settled in meditative concentration, it is like the bright sun suspended in the sky, illuminating all phenomena with clarity;
thus, one is immediately able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly dharmas. This is called "diligence."

This [practice] serves as the antidote to three types of laziness: 1. Diligently practicing moderation in food and sleep, and regulating the inhalation and exhalation of breath, serves as the antidote to the laziness of lack of tranquility.

2. Diligently practicing the cultivation of awareness that all meditative absorptions possess the merit of supernormal powers and wisdom, which can exhaust the source of suffering and accomplish great and wondrous feats, serves as the antidote to the laziness of finding no flavor [in practice].

Laziness. Third, one diligently practices the contemplation that the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the sufferings of the four evil destinies, have not yet been abandoned by me.
This serves as the antidote to the laziness of failing to recognize [the danger] and feeling no fear. By practicing these three antidotes, the mind does not become distracted;
and when there is nothing further to be countered, one is able to give rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), severing delusions and realizing the fruit.
Thus it is. The application of the analogy to the Dharma is easily understood from the text. △ Seventh, the merit of wisdom:
"O bhikṣus, if you possess wisdom, you will have no greedy attachment. You should constantly examine yourselves so as not to allow any lapse."
In this way, one can attain liberation within my Dharma. If it were otherwise, such a person would be neither a seeker of the Path nor a layperson;
they would have no name at all. True wisdom is the sturdy ship that crosses the ocean of old age, sickness, and death;
it is the great bright lamp in the darkness of ignorance; and it is the excellent medicine for all who are ill. To strike down...
It is the sharp axe for the tree of afflictions. Therefore, you should increase your own merit through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
If a person possesses the illumination of wisdom, even though they possess only physical eyes, they are one who sees clearly; this is what is called wisdom.
"If there is wisdom, then there is no greedy attachment. This indicates the merit of true wisdom being free from hindrances;
that is, it refers to being far removed from the hindrance regarding the locus of ultimate reality and the hindrance regarding the locus of worldly affairs.

Because one has severed the ignorance that deludes one regarding the principle, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses do not greedily attach to the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as a self or phenomena. This is called...

It is the removal of obstacles regarding the locus of ultimate reality. Because one has severed the ignorance that deludes one regarding phenomena, the first six consciousnesses do not give rise to craving and attachment toward the objects of the six sense-fields; this is called the removal of obstacles regarding the locus of worldly phenomena.
