To constantly examine oneself so as not to allow for any lapse is a general exhortation to increase the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. This, then, regarding...
In my Dharma, one can attain liberation by means of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), whereby one attains the realization of true wisdom.
One who increases these three wisdoms to realize true wisdom is called a "Path-person" (*mārga-pudgala*). One who has never left the household life is called a "white-robed one" (*avadāta-vastra*).
Now, having already left the household life yet lacking the four types of wisdom, you have lost ground both in advancing and retreating; thus, you have no name. Next, as for the four...
True wisdom is illustrated as follows: the wisdom that perceives the Truth of Suffering is like a sturdy ship; the wisdom that abandons the Truth of Origination is like a great bright lamp;
the wisdom that realizes the Truth of Cessation is like an excellent medicine; and the wisdom that cultivates the Truth of the Path is like a sharp axe.
However, because true wisdom is difficult to realize, one must certainly augment it through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. This is the stage of names.

In the middle stage, the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) increases, whereby one enters the state of stabilizing the mind through the distinct and general mindfulness of characteristics (*vyañjana-artha-nimitta*).

In the stage of contemplative practice (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) increases, whereby one enters the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*). In the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-avasthā*), the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) increases.
One attains the vision of the principle of the Four Noble Truths, gives rise to untainted, true wisdom, and realizes the fruits of the four paths.

Although those with the three types of wisdom within the causal stage have not yet attained the divine eye, and even those liberated by wisdom lack the divine eye, they all clearly perceive the Four Truths and do not fall into false views;
thus, they are persons of clear vision. This is the interpretation according to the meaning of the Tripiṭaka Teaching. As for the Shared Teaching:
To know this by example: because these three vehicles share common expedient means. △ Eighth, ultimate merit:
"O bhikṣus, through various conceptual proliferations, your minds become distracted; though you have left the household life, you have not yet attained liberation."
Therefore, bhikṣus, you should quickly abandon the distracted mind and frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
If you desire to attain the bliss of tranquility (*śānti*), you must only skillfully extinguish the affliction of frivolous proliferation; this is called non-proliferation.
The seven kinds of merit mentioned above are all merits of the skillful means of cultivation. This [next section] demonstrates the self-nature of detachment, which is not a remedial dharma;
therefore, it is called "ultimate merit. True Suchness and Nirvana are pure by their very nature;
they transcend the path of language and the sphere of mental activity. Originally, they are not the domain of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); because of such proliferation...

Because of this argument, it contradicts the bliss of quiescence (*śānti*). Although one who has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) gains true wisdom and perceives the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*), thereby permanently severing the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa-kleśa*), the eighty-one grades of cognitive afflictions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) across the nine stages of the three realms are all formed by the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of beginningless linguistic proliferation (*prapañca*).
These cause the mind to be disturbed and prevent it from acceding to the True and Constant. Therefore:
One must urgently abandon conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) in order to attain the bliss of the quiescence of *nirvāṇa*. What is meant by "thoroughly extinguishing" is this:

by means of the true wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths that has been attained, one repeatedly contemplates the reality through sustained reflection, observing it again and again to purify the seeds and manifestations of karmic consciousness, ensuring they never arise again in the ultimate sense.
This explanation is based on the meaning of the Tripiṭaka; if one were to open [the teaching further]...
To manifest [the truth] by dwelling apart from phenomena is still conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); to see that phenomena are eternally true is not conceptual proliferation.

Furthermore, to possess emptiness while remaining attached to it is still conceptual proliferation; for the Middle Way to be non-empty is not conceptual proliferation. Moreover, to establish a middle by departing from extremes is still conceptual proliferation;
for the extreme to be identical with the middle is not conceptual proliferation. Furthermore, to clarify the Real by contrast with the Provisional—[is likewise conceptual proliferation].

It still involves conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). To "open up the provisional to reveal the real" implies that there is nothing coarse and nothing sublime; this is not yet free from conceptual proliferation.

Furthermore, to speak of the provisional and the real, or of the fundamental and the derivative, is likewise all conceptual proliferation. If the contemplation of the mind arises, both the fundamental and the derivative are severed; this is freedom from conceptual proliferation.
Moreover, to value only silence falls into the view of the ineffable, which still belongs to conceptual proliferation. One must know these four positions.
All these are ineffable; yet, because there are causes and conditions, they can also be spoken of. Whether speaking or not speaking, their nature is inherently equal.
One should not form the dualistic understanding, nor the unitary understanding, nor the understanding that it is both one and two, nor the understanding that it is neither one nor two.
This is indeed the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The section on the True Doctrine is hereby concluded.
△ The third section, the Dissemination, is divided into four parts: first, the dissemination encouraging practice; second, the dissemination of definitive testimony;
third, the dissemination resolving doubts; and fourth, the dissemination of entrustment. This is the first.
"O bhikṣus, regarding all meritorious qualities, you should always be single-minded and abandon all negligence as you would avoid enemies or thieves.
That which was taught for your benefit by the World-Honored One of Great Compassion is now entirely complete; you should simply practice it with diligence."
Whether in the mountains, in a desolate marsh, beneath a tree, in a secluded place, or in a quiet chamber, one should contemplate the Dharma received and not allow it to be forgotten.
One should always exert oneself and cultivate it with diligence; do not die in vain and later fall into regret.
I am like a skilled physician who diagnoses the illness and prescribes the medicine; whether it is taken or not is not the fault of the physician.
I am also like a good guide who leads people onto the path of goodness; that they hear the way and yet do not follow it is not the error of the guide.

"All merits" refers to the three kinds of remedial merits common to worldly dharmas and the eight kinds of great person's merits uncommon to worldly dharmas found within the section on the True Teaching (zhengzongfen). "One should always maintain a single mind" means:

One practices by relying on the mind of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-citta*). "Abandoning all negligence as one would avoid an enemy thief" means remaining far removed from conduct that contradicts single-mindedness (*ekāgra-citta*).

"All that has been taught for the benefit [of others] is already perfected" means that his boundless great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) leaves nothing withheld regarding the Dharma. How, then, is this practiced? It means one should apply oneself to it with diligence.
Where is it practiced? It is said to be among mountains, in empty marshes, beneath trees, in secluded places, or in quiet rooms.

What is it that is practiced? It is said to be mindfulness of the dharmas one has received. For what purpose is it practiced? It is said to be so as not to let them be forgotten or lost. By what means is it practiced?
This means that one must always exert oneself and cultivate with diligence. If one has not yet entered the truth, all such efforts are called empty deaths.

If one considers a small attainment to be sufficient, there will surely be regret later; once regret arises, what can be done? In terms of extinguishing evil and uprooting suffering, the Buddha is like a skilled physician;
in terms of generating goodness and bestowing happiness, he is like a virtuous guide. The Buddha does not fail sentient beings; it is the sentient beings who...
It would be a great loss to the Buddha; how tragic this would be! △ Second, the certification and resolution for the circulation [of the teaching]:
"If you have any doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths, such as suffering and the rest, you should quickly ask about them.
Do not harbor doubts and fail to seek their resolution. At that time, the World-Honored One made this proclamation three times, yet no one asked a question. Why was this so?

Because the assembly was free from doubt, at that time Ānanda, observing the minds of the assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the moon might be made hot, and the sun might be made cold;
but what the Buddha has taught regarding the Four Noble Truths cannot be otherwise. What the Buddha has taught as the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure.
Accumulation (the Truth of Origination) is truly the cause, and there is no other cause. If suffering is to be extinguished, it is precisely through this cause."
Cessation. Because of the cessation of the cause, there is the cessation of the fruit. The path leading to the cessation of suffering is truly the authentic path; there is no other path.
World-Honored One, these bhikṣus have attained certainty and are free from doubt regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Although the teachings of the Tathāgata throughout his entire life are numerous in their principles and meanings, they are fully subsumed within the Four Noble Truths.

The two truths of suffering and its origin fully encompass the causes and effects of the mundane world, while the two truths of cessation and the path fully encompass the causes and effects of the supramundane.

Therefore, if one harbors doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths, one will harbor doubts regarding all phenomena; conversely, if one has no doubts regarding the Four Noble Truths, then [one has no doubts regarding anything].
One shall attain freedom from doubt regarding all phenomena. This is why, as his passing approaches, he earnestly proclaims three times:

to profoundly demonstrate that apart from the Four Noble Truths, there is no other teaching. Within this text, the meaning is subsumed under three sections, manifesting the certainty and absence of doubt.
From the beginning up to "not seeking a definitive resolution" is the first gate, the Gate of Manifestation through Expedient Means.
This is because these Four Truths are what practitioners constantly observe and rely upon to initiate their practice.
From "At that time, the World-Honored One" up to "the assembly had no further doubts" is the second gate, the Gate of Fulfillment and Accomplishment. Within this, there are three proclamations.

The phrase "turning the wheel of Dharma" demonstrates the fulfillment of accomplishment through manifestation. The phrase "no one asks questions" demonstrates the fulfillment of accomplishment through the realization of the Dharma.
The phrase "the assembly has no doubt" demonstrates the fulfillment of accomplishment through the severance of [doubt regarding] merit.
From Ānanda up to "certainty and freedom from doubt," this is the third gate of analytical exposition. Ānanda...
*Da* (also transliterated as *Aniruddha*, *Aniruddhu*, or *Anuruddha*)—these are merely variations in the pronunciation of the Sanskrit sound.
This translates as "Free from Poverty," "Non-extinction," or "As One Wishes. In the past, during a time of famine, he offered a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha;
consequently, for ninety-one kalpas, he was reborn among gods and humans, always [enjoying prosperity].
He has enjoyed blessings and happiness that remain undiminished to this day; because his every wish is fulfilled as he desires, he has acquired this name.

As the foremost in the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he is able to observe the minds of all beings and explain them with definitive discernment. The moon is the essence of the Great Yin, and is therefore cold.

The sun is hot because it is the essence of solar radiance. However, this container-world of the environment and its inhabitants is entirely a manifestation of our own *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only);

it is the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of consciousness and lacks any inherent reality. Therefore, those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) can cause the moon to become hot and the sun to become cold.

As for the Four Noble Truths taught by the Buddha, they are likewise... [the assembly]... (Note: The source text appears to be a fragment, likely from a commentary on Yogācāra philosophy. The final sentence is incomplete, but the core argument concerns the illusory nature of the phenomenal world as a projection of consciousness.)
The principle that the nature of the mind is thus produced is a fundamental law; this principle is immutable.

Just as with the Truth of Suffering, throughout the twenty-five realms of existence within the three worlds—from the Avīci Hell below to the Naivasamjñānāsamjñāyatana Heaven above—although the differences between ascending and descending states are vast, [the nature remains unchanged].

Nevertheless, there is nothing that is not transformed by the four marks [of existence] or oppressed by the eight sufferings; how, then, could one cause it to be happy? As for the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*):

the two delusions of views and mental afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), along with the three types of outflowing karma—wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable—are precisely the causes that draw one into rebirth within the triple world;
how could there be any other cause? As for the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): when the cause ceases, the fruit of suffering follows in cessation; how could this be otherwise?

It is not a state of non-quiescence or unconditioned bliss. Just as with the Truth of the Path, the triad of ethical discipline (*śīla*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) can sever both the cause and the fruit of suffering, leading to the state where there is no suffering. What other path could there be?

Since these four are all examined and real, and not false, they are called "Truths" (*satya*). The Buddha spoke them according to reality, and the bhikṣus likewise understand them according to reality; therefore, they are certain and free from doubt.
△ Third, the section on Dispelling Doubts and Promulgating [the Teaching], which is also threefold: first, revealing remaining doubts; second, severing those various doubts;
third, reiterating the characteristics of conditioned impermanence to exhort practice. Now, the first.
Among this assembly, those who have not yet accomplished what was to be done will feel grief upon seeing the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Those who have newly entered the Dharma, upon hearing what the Buddha has taught, will immediately attain deliverance—just as one who sees a flash of lightning at night can suddenly see the path.
But those who have already accomplished what was to be done and have crossed over the sea of suffering will simply think: "The World-Honored One has passed into parinirvāṇa."
"How rapid! This is still a differentiated statement of Ānanda. Within it, there are three kinds of differentiation:

first, those for whom what was to be done is not yet accomplished, referring to those who have attained the first, second, or third fruits, because their afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) have not been completely severed.

One should feel a sense of compassion, as was the case with Ānanda’s sorrow and other such instances. Second, regarding those who first enter the Dharma: this refers to those at the stages of the inner and outer ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

Because the power of their contemplative practice is profound, upon hearing the Buddha-dharma for the first time, they swiftly perceive the Path (*darśanamārga*), like seeing a flash of lightning at night;
there is no further delay, for the sixteen moments of mind that constitute the perception of the Path do not exceed a single *kṣaṇa*.
Therefore [it is so]. Third, regarding "those who have already accomplished what was to be done," this refers to the Arhats.

Having exhausted the afflictions of both views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), they have forever transcended the ocean of suffering of the triple world; thus, they no longer possess worldly affection or feelings of grief.
Yet, not yet knowing that the Buddha is truly imperishable, they ask why his *parinirvāṇa* is so sudden. △ Second, to sever their various doubts.
Although Ānanda spoke these words, those in the assembly had all thoroughly understood the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
Desiring to cause this great multitude to attain firm stability, the World-Honored One, out of a heart of great compassion, spoke again to the assembly:

"O bhikṣus, do not harbor grief or distress. Even if I were to remain in the world for an eon, this assembly would still eventually perish. Where there is an assembly, there is no escaping separation."
In the end, it cannot be obtained. The dharmas for self-benefit and benefiting others are all fully complete. If I were to remain for a long time, there would be no further benefit.
Those among the denizens of heaven and the human realm who were to be delivered have all already been delivered;

as for those not yet delivered, the causes and conditions for their deliverance have also already been established. From this day forward, my disciples shall practice this in succession; this is the Tathāgata’s [instruction].
The Dharma-body thus comes to abide eternally and never perishes.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: because one realizes these four truths and thereby attains the fruit of sainthood (*ārya-phala*), they are called the "Noble Truths.

Furthermore, although this principle is inherently so, it is only the sages who fully comprehend it; therefore, they are called the "Noble Truths. Although the assembly has all thoroughly understood them, yet as...
His compassionate heart is now pure and profound; he speaks again for the sake of the multitude so that all future beings may forever sever their remaining doubts.

This section is also divided into three parts. First, from "Do not harbor sorrowful distress" to "it would be of no further benefit," he severs the doubt regarding the cessation of the compassionate sentiment that arises from the perception that one’s unfinished tasks remain unaccomplished.
Since the dharmas for both self-benefit and benefiting others are already fully complete, [there is no longer any need for such concern].
"You may then rely upon this to cultivate the Way. That there must be separation when meeting is simply the nature of worldly phenomena;
it is only natural. Furthermore, my long stay here will be of no benefit to you, so why harbor such grief?

Second, from 'those who should be saved' to 'attaining the conditions for deliverance,' this refers to severing the doubts regarding the vision of the Path, like a flash of lightning. For instance, there was a doubt that arose while the Buddha was staying..."
In times past, upon hearing the teaching, they all attained deliverance. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there was no means by which they could see the Path;

therefore, I now explain: those who were to be delivered have already been delivered by me. Even as for those not yet delivered, I have already established the causes and conditions for their deliverance.
When these causes and conditions reach fruition, do not grieve that you will not see the Path. (3) From this day forward, until...
It is not extinguished. This dispels the doubt as to why there would be such haste in attaining cessation through extinction (*uccheda-nirvāṇa*).

Since the disciples transmit and practice this in succession, the aspect of maintenance (*sthiti*) within the causal stage (*hetu-bhāga*) remains undestroyed. Since the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is eternally present and does not perish, the aspect of maintenance within the resultant stage (*phala-bhāga*) remains undestroyed.

When both cause and effect are eternal, how can one say it is quickly extinguished? However, this is still addressed to those of provisional capacity; therefore, for the time being, only five [aspects] are taught.
The Dharma-body is taught to be eternally abiding. If one enters into the reality [of this teaching], then even the transformation bodies must be eternal;
thus, the single assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly without dispersing, which is not a deception of me. △ Third, explaining the characteristics of conditioned impermanence to exhort practice.
Therefore, you should know that all in the world is impermanent; where there is meeting, there must be separation. Do not harbor grief or distress; such is the nature of the world.
You should apply yourself with diligent effort to seek liberation early, using the light of wisdom to extinguish the darkness of ignorance. The world is truly precarious and fragile.
That which is not firm has now attained extinction for me, like the removal of a malignant disease. This body is something to be abandoned;
it is a vessel of evil, a mere conventional designation for what is called "the body. It is submerged in the great ocean of old age, sickness, birth, and death.
What wise person, having brought about its cessation, would not rejoice, just as one who slays a hostile enemy?
This passage contains two intentions. From the beginning up to "not firm and stable" correctly elucidates the gate of contemplation on impermanence, exhorting diligent practice.
From "I have now attained extinction" onwards, it serves as a personal testimony. [This refers to] the Buddha’s wondrous form-body.
The true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is equal [to all], manifesting as the adornment of immeasurable merits;

yet, to say that it is a sinful thing and to use metaphors such as a malignant disease or a hostile thief is to show its identity with that of ordinary beings, thereby causing them to be vigilant and self-reflective. This concludes the third section:
Dispelling Doubts and Promulgating [the Teaching]. △ Fourth: Entrusting and Promulgating.
"You, bhikṣus, should always with a single mind diligently seek the way out.
All phenomena in the world, whether conditioned or unconditioned, possess the nature of decay and instability. You should now cease; do not speak further. The time is drawing to a close."
"I am about to enter parinirvāṇa; this is my final instruction.
You must always maintain a single-minded focus. This is an entrustment to abide in true wisdom (*bhūta-prajñā*). "Diligently seek the path beyond [suffering].

This is an entrustment to practice through skillful means (*upāya*). Because true wisdom is difficult to attain, he exhorts them to cultivate it with vigor. [This concerns] the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The realm of desire is characterized by movement; the realms of form and formlessness are characterized by non-movement.
Although there is this distinction between movement and stillness, all are collectively subject to impermanence and selflessness; one must therefore contemplate renunciation. Do not speak further.

This is an exhortation to cease the three types of action, thereby becoming a vessel for the realization of quiescence and selflessness. "The time is about to pass" indicates that one should return to extinction. Not... [text ends].

To depart from the Middle Way as the ultimate goal is the final instruction; this is the clear manifestation of his bequeathed teaching, the most supreme and essential among all methods for upholding the Dharma.
Alas! How profound was his earnest compassion in these final moments! For those who are disciples:
It is fitting that this be engraved upon one's bones and inscribed upon one's liver.

Before I, Xu, had left the household life, I read this *Teaching Left Behind* (Śālistamba-sūtra) and immediately understood that every character was written with blood and tears.

Having received the tonsure and the dyed robes, I have not dared to forget it. Yet, what I regret is that my wisdom is shallow and my afflictions are deep; for more than twenty years, I have idly passed the time, achieving nothing at all.
Being neither a man of the Way nor a layman, I now stroke my heart in self-reproach and look into the mirror with a sense of shame.
I am ashamed that, misled by empty fame, I have erroneously received such veneration. Yet, at the earnest request of the layman Fu Dunshen, I have been compelled to explain this sutra.
Alas! I am unable to cultivate the merits of either the mundane or supramundane realms;
to merely employ words and letters as a gift of Dharma—how is this any different from the birds that preach the Dharma to the devas? Nevertheless, through this single opening of...
Illuminating my own inability to be stingy with this merit, I dedicate it toward the Western Pure Land.
